claim: Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens were conducted in 21 OSCC cell lines, primarily derived from Asians.
source: We conducted genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens in 21 OSCC cell lines, primarily derived from Asians, to identify genetic vulnerabilities that can be explored as therapeutic targets.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number and origin of cell lines screened.

claim: Many previously identified OSCC-related cancer genes are non-essential and could have limited therapeutic value.
source: We identify known and novel fitness genes and demonstrate that many previously identified OSCC-related cancer genes are non-essential and could have limited therapeutic value, while other fitness genes warrant further investigation for their potential as therapeutic targets.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from the screening results.

claim: A distinctive dependency on YAP1 and WWTR1 of the Hippo pathway was validated.
source: We validate a distinctive dependency on YAP1 and WWTR1 of the Hippo pathway, where the lost-of-fitness effect of one paralog can be compensated only in a subset of lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this validation finding.

claim: OSCCs with WWTR1 dependency signature are significantly associated with biomarkers of favorable response toward immunotherapy.
source: We also discover that OSCCs with WWTR1 dependency signature are significantly associated with biomarkers of favorable response toward immunotherapy.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this association finding.

claim: OSCC is especially prevalent among Asian countries.
source: The commonest subtype, oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is especially prevalent among Asian countries (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Bray et al., 2018.

claim: OSCC has been associated with distinct risk habits such as betel quid chewing, tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption.
source: OSCC has been associated with distinct risk habits such as betel quid chewing, tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption (Shield et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Shield et al., 2017.

claim: The 5-year survival rate for OSCC is about 50%.
source: The 5-year survival rate for OSCC is about 50% (Kumar et al., 2016) and surgery remains the mainstay of treatment.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016.

claim: Surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for OSCC.
source: The 5-year survival rate for OSCC is about 50% (Kumar et al., 2016) and surgery remains the mainstay of treatment.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016.

claim: Cetuximab is used in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced OSCC.
source: Cetuximab, an inhibitor of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), is used in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced OSCC (Vermorken et al., 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Vermorken et al., 2008.

claim: The improvement in survival with cetuximab remains marginal.
source: However, the improvement in survival remains marginal (Vermorken et al., 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Vermorken et al., 2008.

claim: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of advanced and metastatic OSCC.
source: More recently, immune checkpoint inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of advanced and metastatic OSCC (Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2019.

claim: Clinical trial outcomes showed an average objective response rate of only 13–36% for checkpoint inhibitors in OSCC.
source: Although an improvement in patients' outcome is anticipated with the advancement of immunotherapy, clinical trial outcomes showed an average objective response rate of only 13–36% (Bauml et al., 2017; Burtness et al., 2019; Ferris et al., 2016), and the factors determining response towards checkpoint inhibitors are still largely unknown.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Bauml et al., 2017; Burtness et al., 2019; Ferris et al., 2016.

claim: The factors determining response towards checkpoint inhibitors are still largely unknown.
source: Although an improvement in patients' outcome is anticipated with the advancement of immunotherapy, clinical trial outcomes showed an average objective response rate of only 13–36% (Bauml et al., 2017; Burtness et al., 2019; Ferris et al., 2016), and the factors determining response towards checkpoint inhibitors are still largely unknown.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Bauml et al., 2017; Burtness et al., 2019; Ferris et al., 2016.

claim: Genomic sequencing technology has enabled the delineation of the comprehensive mutational and transcriptomic landscape of OSCC.
source: Genomic sequencing technology has enabled the delineation of the comprehensive mutational and transcriptomic landscape of cancers, including OSCC (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Pickering et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Pickering et al., 2013.

claim: The functional significance of most genetic alterations in OSCC remains unclear.
source: However, the functional significance of most of these genetic alterations remains unclear and little is known about their value as therapeutic targets for OSCC.
evidence: The statement is made in the context of discussing genomic sequencing findings.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 technology has high specificity and efficiency compared to RNAi.
source: More recently, essential genes have been identified through the use of CRISPR-Cas9 technology due to its high specificity and efficiency compared to RNAi (Gerhards and Rottenberg, 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Gerhards and Rottenberg, 2018.

claim: Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens have shown promising outcomes in identifying novel cancer-specific vulnerabilities that are useful drug targets.
source: Several studies using genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen have already shown promising outcome in identifying novel cancer-specific vulnerabilities that are useful drug targets (Steinhart et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), as well as improving the understanding of drug mechanism of action (Barazas et al., 2018; Hou et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Steinhart et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Barazas et al., 2018; Hou et al., 2017.

claim: The Cancer Dependency Map project has conducted CRISPR-Cas9 screens on a large number of cell lines including some OSCC models.
source: The Cancer Dependency Map project (a consortium effort by the Wellcome Sanger Institute and the Broad Institute) have conducted CRISPR-Cas9 screen on a large number of cell lines including some OSCC models (Behan et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Behan et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2017.

claim: There is a lack of representation of Asian OSCC in existing CRISPR screens.
source: However, there is a lack of representation of Asians OSCC, such as those associated with betel quid chewing habit, one of the major risk factors of OSCC in many Asian countries (Shield et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Shield et al., 2017.

claim: Comparison of genomics data across different populations has revealed distinctive features in the different populations.
source: Further, the comparison of genomics data across different populations has revealed distinctive features in the different populations (Chai et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Chai et al., 2020.

claim: The study performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens on 21 highly annotated OSCC cell lines, most of which are unique models derived from Asian patients.
source: To identify genetic vulnerabilities in OSCC, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens on 21 highly annotated OSCC cell lines, most of which are unique models derived from Asian patients (Fadlullah et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Fadlullah et al., 2016.

claim: The study contributes to approximately one-third of the OSCC functional genetic screens currently available globally.
source: Our study contributes to approximately one-third of the OSCC functional genetic screens currently available globally, expanding the representation of this heterogeneous disease (Behan et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Behan et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2017.

claim: YAP1 and WWTR1 show mutually exclusive dependency in different subsets of OSCC models.
source: We validated the essentiality of Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1) and WW domain-containing transcription regulator protein 1 (WWTR1) and revealed mutually exclusive dependency and compensable functions of these paralogs in different subsets of OSCC models.
evidence: The statement is based on validation experiments described in the study.

claim: OSCC tumors with a gene expression signature similar to WWTR1-dependent cell lines showed significant enrichment of immune-related pathways.
source: Among which, OSCC resembling the WWTR1-dependent cell lines showed significant enrichment of immune-related pathways and are associated with biomarkers of response towards checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression analysis of OSCC tumors.

claim: 918 non-core fitness genes were shortlisted after filtering out core fitness genes.
source: Overall, among the 18,010 genes screened, 2539 (14%) were found to be significant MAGeCK hits in at least one cell line and following the removal of core fitness genes (Supplementary file 2), 918 context-specific fitness genes were shortlisted for further prioritization (Figure 1B).
evidence: The statement is supported by data analysis results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: About 40% (366 genes) of the 918 non-core fitness genes were uniquely essential in a single cell line.
source: About 40% (366 genes) were uniquely essential in a single cell line, while the remaining 60% (552 genes) were essential in at least two cell lines, hence are recurrent context-specific essentialities (Figure 1C).
evidence: The statement is supported by data analysis results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pathways such as ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis and cellular senescence are common across all cell lines.
source: Whilst pathways such as ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis and cellular senescence are common across all cell lines, pathways such as NF-kappa B and MAPK signaling pathways are selectively enriched only in subsets of cell lines.
evidence: The statement is based on pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Drugs targeting PIK3CA and CDK6 are already in clinical trials for HNSCC treatment.
source: For example, drugs targeting PIK3CA and CDK6 are already in clinical trials for HNSCC treatment [NCT01816984, NCT02537223, NCT03356223, NCT03356587].
evidence: The statement is supported by clinical trial identifiers.

claim: More than half of the 44 HNSCC cancer genes with driver mutations were dispensable for OSCC survival.
source: We also examined the dependency profile of 44 cancer genes with driver mutations known to be associated with HNSCC (Bailey et al., 2018; Martincorena et al., 2018; Figure 2B) and found that more than half of these cancer genes were dispensable for OSCC survival.
evidence: The statement is supported by data analysis results shown in Figure 2B and citations to Bailey et al., 2018; Martincorena et al., 2018.

claim: Dependencies on mutated PIK3CA were observed in four OSCC cell lines with hotspot mutations.
source: Dependencies on mutated PIK3CA were observed in four OSCC cell lines with a hotspot mutation in E545K (BICR10), Q546R (ORL-150) and H1047R (HSC-2), and to a lesser extent, in ORL-115 with H1047L mutation.
evidence: The statement is based on CRISPR score analysis of cell lines with PIK3CA mutations.

claim: HSC-4, which harbors the same E545K mutation as BICR10, did not show any dependency on the mutated PIK3CA.
source: Intriguingly, HSC-4, which harbors the same E545K mutation as BICR10, did not show any dependency on the mutated PIK3CA, this is consistent with findings from Project Score (Behan et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by CRISPR score data and a citation to Behan et al., 2019.

claim: A splice site driver mutation in PTEN co-occurred in HSC-4 and may have counteracted the oncogene addiction effect on the mutated PIK3CA.
source: A splice site driver mutation in PTEN co-occurred in HSC-4 and may have counteracted the oncogene addiction effect on the mutated PIK3CA, as suggested previously in breast cancer (Lazaridis et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Lazaridis et al., 2019.

claim: Dependency on NFE2L2 was observed in Ho-1-u-1 and BICR10.
source: Dependency on NFE2L2 was observed in Ho-1-u-1 and BICR10 however the mechanism of activating this oxidative pathway differed between these two cell lines.
evidence: The statement is based on CRISPR score analysis.

claim: Ho-1-u-1 has a hotspot mutation (E82D) in NFE2L2 that has been shown to enhance its transcriptional activity and promoting cell proliferation.
source: Oncogene addiction is observed for Ho-1-u-1 with a hotspot mutation (E82D) in NFE2L2, that has been shown to enhance its transcriptional activity and promoting cell proliferation (Shibata et al., 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Shibata et al., 2008.

claim: BICR10 harbors an inactivating mutation on KEAP1 (R320Q) that has been reported to stabilize NRF2 and enhances cell fitness.
source: On the other hand, BICR10 harbors an inactivating mutation on KEAP1 (R320Q) a negative regulator of NFE2L2. The R320Q mutation has been reported to stabilize NRF2 (encoded by NFE2L2) and enhances cell fitness as reported previously in lung cancer (Hast et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Hast et al., 2014.

claim: The only cell line that shows dependency on HRAS is ORL-214 which carries a mutation in HRAS (G12C).
source: Finally, the only cell line that shows dependency on HRAS is ORL-214 which carries a mutation in HRAS (G12C).
evidence: The statement is based on CRISPR score analysis.

claim: ZFP36L1 with truncating mutation at S324 in ORL-48 showed preferential dependency.
source: Another gene, encoding ZFP36L1 with truncating mutation at S324 in ORL-48 also showed preferential dependency, suggesting that the effect of this mutation should be studied further.
evidence: The statement is based on CRISPR score analysis.

claim: The NF-kB signaling pathway is significantly enriched among betel-quid-associated OSCC.
source: Of the 110 fitness genes uniquely seen in betel-quid-associated OSCC, the NF-kB signaling pathway stands out as one of the significantly enriched pathway.
evidence: The statement is based on pathway enrichment analysis of betel-quid-associated OSCC.

claim: Three out of four (75%) of the NF-kB pathway genes unique to betel quid-associated OSCC (NFKB2, TNFAIP3, and TRIM25) were not found among the screened OSCC models in DepMap and Project Score.
source: When cross checking with the DepMap and Project Score data, three out of four (75%) of these genes (NFKB2, TNFAIP3, and TRIM25) were not found among the screened OSCC models, which were mostly derived from Caucasians, or from Asians not known to chew betel quid.
evidence: The statement is based on comparison with DepMap and Project Score data.

claim: Extract from the areca nut of betel quid can directly activate the NF-kB signaling pathway, favoring OSCC cells survival.
source: Interestingly, our findings are coherent with previous studies from Taiwan and India, where betel quid chewing is common, which have demonstrated that extract from the areca nut of betel quid can directly activate the NF-kB signaling pathway, favoring OSCC cells survival (Chiang et al., 2008; Islam et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2008; Islam et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2005.

claim: 45 genes from the 918 fitness genes fall into tractability group 1.
source: From the 918 genes, 45 genes fall into the tractability group 1, some examples of genes in this group include EGFR, PIK3CA, CDK4, and CDK6, where anticancer drugs targeting these genes are already approved or clinical trials for the treatment of HNSCC are on-going, demonstrating the robustness of our results.
evidence: The statement is based on tractability assessment analysis.

claim: About 70% of the 918 genes belong to tractability group 3 (least tractable or lacking evidence).
source: However, about 70% of the 918 genes belong to tractability group 3 (least tractable or lacking evidence) where significant efforts in understanding their structure and function would be necessary to evaluate their tractability.
evidence: The statement is based on tractability assessment analysis.

claim: YAP1 or WWTR1 amplifications occur in approximately 19% of HNSCC.
source: Furthermore, YAP1 or WWTR1 amplifications occur in approximately 19% of HNSCC (YAP1–5.5%, WWTR1–14.3%), which puts it among the top five cancers with the highest amplification of these genes amongst 33 cancer types (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: YAP1 and WWTR1 are paralogs with ~46–60% similarity in their amino acid sequence.
source: YAP1 and WWTR1 (also known as TAZ) are transcription co-activators, which are the major effectors of the Hippo pathway (Guo and Teng, 2015; Wang et al., 2018). YAP1 and WWTR1 are paralogs with ~46–60% similarity in their amino acid sequence (Guo and Teng, 2015).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Guo and Teng, 2015; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: There were seven lines that were highly dependent on YAP1.
source: There were seven lines that were highly dependent on YAP1 (ORL-48, ORL-136, ORL-156, ORL-204, ORL-207, SAS, SCC-9), four highly dependent on WWTR1 (ORL-174, ORL-188, ORL-214, PE/CA-PJ15), while the other eight were not dependent on either (Figure 3A).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Four lines were highly dependent on WWTR1.
source: There were seven lines that were highly dependent on YAP1 (ORL-48, ORL-136, ORL-156, ORL-204, ORL-207, SAS, SCC-9), four highly dependent on WWTR1 (ORL-174, ORL-188, ORL-214, PE/CA-PJ15), while the other eight were not dependent on either (Figure 3A).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Eight lines were not dependent on either YAP1 or WWTR1.
source: There were seven lines that were highly dependent on YAP1 (ORL-48, ORL-136, ORL-156, ORL-204, ORL-207, SAS, SCC-9), four highly dependent on WWTR1 (ORL-174, ORL-188, ORL-214, PE/CA-PJ15), while the other eight were not dependent on either (Figure 3A).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of the WWTR1-dependent cell lines have copy number amplification for genes on 3q25-28.
source: Notably, WWTR1 gene locus (3q25) is at close proximity to the locus of PIK3CA, SOX2 and TP63 at 3q26-28, whereby their focal amplification is frequently reported in HNSCC (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C). The majority of the WWTR1-dependent cell lines have copy number amplification for these genes on 3q25-28 (Figure 3A), but only WWTR1 CRISPR scores are significantly different between those with and without copy number amplification (p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, and a citation to The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015.

claim: Only WWTR1 CRISPR scores are significantly different between those with and without copy number amplification on 3q25-28 (p<0.001).
source: The majority of the WWTR1-dependent cell lines have copy number amplification for these genes on 3q25-28 (Figure 3A), but only WWTR1 CRISPR scores are significantly different between those with and without copy number amplification (p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: An enrichment of PIK3CA mutations (p=0.0003) was observed among cell lines that are neither dependent on YAP1 or WWTR1.
source: Notably, we also observed an enrichment of PIK3CA mutations (p=0.0003) among cell lines that are neither dependent on YAP1 or WWTR1, whereby five out of six such lines have PIK3CA hotspot mutations (BICR10, HSC-2, HSC-4, ORL-115, and ORL-150) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: None of the 21 OSCC cell lines shows copy number amplification of YAP1 or neighbouring genes on the chromosome 11q22.
source: In our study, despite having cell lines dependent on YAP1, none of the 21 OSCC cell lines shows copy number amplification of YAP1 or neighbouring genes on the chromosome 11q22.
evidence: The statement is based on copy number analysis of the cell lines.

claim: YAP1 depletion in ORL-48 resulted in significant reduction in viable cells.
source: Consistently, YAP1 depletion in ORL-48 resulted in significant reduction in viable cells, to a level comparable to the depletion of PLK1 (Figure 4A), and this was reflected in the increase in apoptotic cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4B.

claim: WWTR1 depletion in ORL-214 showed significantly lower percentage of viable cells when compared with the control.
source: Further, WWTR1 depletion in ORL-214 showed significantly lower percentage of viable cells when compared with the control, as well as significant increase in apoptotic cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of either YAP1 or WWTR1 did not affect the survival of HSC-2.
source: By contrast, depletion of either YAP1 or WWTR1 did not affect the survival of HSC-2, as confirmed by the apoptotic assay (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4B.

claim: The population of BICR10 and HSC-2 with the double knockout of both YAP1 and WWTR1 depleted drastically.
source: The co-competition assays showed that the population of BICR10 and HSC-2 with the double knockout of both YAP1 and WWTR1 depleted drastically (Figure 5B) compared to when each gene was knocked-out individually (Figure 3C).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 3C.

claim: In YAP1/WWTR1 compensable subset of cell lines, the paralogs can compensate for the function of one another to activate the downstream mechanisms required to maintain cell fitness.
source: This suggests that in this YAP1/WWTR1 compensable subset of cell lines, the paralogs can compensate for the function of one another to activate the downstream mechanisms required to maintain cell fitness.
evidence: The statement is based on the double knockout experiment results.

claim: 41 OSCC tumors (13%) had high YAP1 dependency signature score (>0.5).
source: To define representative 'core' samples, we found 41 OSCC tumors (13%) with high YAP1 dependency signature score (>0.5); 30 OSCC (9.5%) with high WWTR1 dependency signature score (>0.5) and 34 OSCC (11%) with high Compensable signature score (>0.5).
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression signature analysis of TCGA OSCC tumors.

claim: 30 OSCC tumors (9.5%) had high WWTR1 dependency signature score (>0.5).
source: To define representative 'core' samples, we found 41 OSCC tumors (13%) with high YAP1 dependency signature score (>0.5); 30 OSCC (9.5%) with high WWTR1 dependency signature score (>0.5) and 34 OSCC (11%) with high Compensable signature score (>0.5).
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression signature analysis of TCGA OSCC tumors.

claim: 34 OSCC tumors (11%) had high Compensable signature score (>0.5).
source: To define representative 'core' samples, we found 41 OSCC tumors (13%) with high YAP1 dependency signature score (>0.5); 30 OSCC (9.5%) with high WWTR1 dependency signature score (>0.5) and 34 OSCC (11%) with high Compensable signature score (>0.5).
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression signature analysis of TCGA OSCC tumors.

claim: YAP1-dependent cell lines and tumors showed enrichment in hallmarks related to cell cycle, such as the E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, MYC targets, and DNA repair pathways.
source: YAP1-dependent cell lines and tumors showed enrichment in hallmarks related to cell cycle, such as the E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, MYC targets, and DNA repair pathways (Figure 6C).
evidence: The statement is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The transcription factors E2F and MYC are critical downstream regulators of YAP/TEAD-mediated activation of cell cycle genes.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that have demonstrated that the transcription factors E2F and MYC are critical downstream regulators of YAP/TEAD-mediated activation of cell cycle genes (Kapoor et al., 2014; Pattschull et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Kapoor et al., 2014; Pattschull et al., 2019.

claim: OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score showed high expression of genes in several hallmarks related to immunity.
source: While OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score showed high expression of genes in several hallmarks related to immunity, such as the interferon responses, inflammatory responses and the complement pathway.
evidence: The statement is based on GSEA results.

claim: WWTR1 may play a role in immunity by upregulating PD-L1 expression.
source: This association is aligned with the recent findings that WWTR1 may play a role in immunity by upregulating PD-L1 expression (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018.

claim: Cell lines and tumors with high Compensable signature score showed enrichment in several metabolism-related hallmarks.
source: On the other hand, cell lines and tumors with high Compensable signature score showed enrichment in several metabolism-related hallmarks, such as fatty acid metabolism and xenobiotic metabolism.
evidence: The statement is based on GSEA results.

claim: All three YAP1/WWTR1 compensable cell lines (BICR10, HSC-2 and HSC-4) harbor PIK3CA mutation.
source: Notably, all three YAP1/WWTR1 compensable cell lines (BICR10, HSC-2 and HSC-4) harbor PIK3CA mutation, and that alterations in the PI3K signaling pathway have been linked to multiple metabolic dysregulations in cancer (Hao et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is based on mutation analysis and supported by a citation to Hao et al., 2016.

claim: OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score showed significantly lower stromal infiltration, but higher immune infiltration compared to the other two groups.
source: Using the stromal and immune signature defined previously (Yoshihara et al., 2013), ssGSEA enrichment scores revealed that OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score showed significantly lower stromal signature, but higher immune signature, when compared with OSCC of high YAP1 dependency or Compensable signature scores (Figure 6D).
evidence: The statement is supported by ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 6D and a citation to Yoshihara et al., 2013.

claim: OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were associated with significantly enriched interferon-gamma (IFNγ) response signatures and reduced transforming growth factor-beta (TGFβ) response.
source: Next, we also assessed the other immune-related scores from previous work (Thorsson et al., 2018) and confirmed that these OSCC were associated with significantly enriched interferon-gamma (IFNγ) response signatures and reduced transforming growth factor-beta (TGFβ) response (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The statement is supported by immune signature analysis shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B, and a citation to Thorsson et al., 2018.

claim: OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score possess significantly higher cytolytic T cells (CD8) score than the other two groups.
source: Consistent with that, they also possess significantly higher cytolytic T cells (CD8) score than the other two groups (Figure 6E).
evidence: The statement is supported by immune signature analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The PD-L1 mRNA expression of the OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were significantly higher than the other two groups.
source: Interestingly, the PD-L1 mRNA expression and the 18-gene T-cell inflamed gene expression profile (GEP) enrichment scores of the OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were significantly higher than the other two groups (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: The statement is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The 18-gene T-cell inflamed GEP enrichment scores of the OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were significantly higher than the other two groups.
source: Interestingly, the PD-L1 mRNA expression and the 18-gene T-cell inflamed gene expression profile (GEP) enrichment scores of the OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were significantly higher than the other two groups (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: The statement is supported by ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: OSCC with high WWTR1 dependency signature score were associated with higher tumor mutational burden (TMB) albeit not statistically significant when compared with the other two groups.
source: They were also associated with higher tumor mutational burden (TMB) albeit not statistically significant when compared with the other two groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The statement is supported by TMB analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: qPCR results revealed strongest suppression of PD-L1 gene expression upon WWTR1 knockout, but remain largely unchanged when the other genes were knockout (PIK3CA, TP63, and SOX2).
source: To ensure that the association with immune signatures seen is specific to WWTR1 but not caused by other co-amplified genes in 3q25-28 (such as PIK3CA, TP63, and SOX2), we examined the changes in gene expression level of PD-L1 upon depletion of WWTR1 and other co-amplified genes. qPCR results revealed strongest suppression of PD-L1 gene expression upon WWTR1 knockout, but remain largely unchanged when the other genes were knockout (PIK3CA, TP63, and SOX2) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: A significant correlation of WWTR1 gene expression with PD-L1 expression was observed, but no correlation in gene expression was seen between PIK3CA, TP63 or SOX2 and PD-L1.
source: We also examined a microarray dataset from Hiemer et al., 2015 and showed that a significant correlation of WWTR1 gene expression with PD-L1 expression was observed, but no correlation in gene expression was seen between PIK3CA, TP63 or SOX2 and PD-L1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and a citation to Hiemer et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of the cell lines used in this study were from Asian patients where OSCC is more prevalent.
source: The majority of the cell lines used in this study were from Asian patients where OSCC is more prevalent, and where causative factors include betel quid chewing in addition to smoking that is more often found in Caucasian patients (Cheong et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Cheong et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2016.

claim: 918 fitness genes were identified in OSCC.
source: Here, we identified 918 fitness genes in OSCC.
evidence: The statement is based on the CRISPR screen analysis results.

claim: About 5% (45/918) of the fitness genes are highly tractable with approved drugs, or have drugs that are in late-stage of clinical testing.
source: Notably, we showed that about 5% (45/918) of these genes are highly tractable with approved drugs, or have drugs that are in late-stage of clinical testing, demonstrating that these screens could help to prioritize drugs that could be repurposed for OSCC treatment.
evidence: The statement is based on tractability assessment analysis.

claim: Candidate genes such as those relating to the cell cycle (CKAP5, KPNB1, RAN, TPX2, and KIF11) were also identified in previous genome-wide RNAi screens.
source: We compared our screens with previous genome-wide RNAi screens and found that candidate genes such as those relating to the cell cycle (CKAP5, KPNB1, RAN, TPX2, and KIF11) were also identified in our dataset (Martens-de Kemp et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Martens-de Kemp et al., 2013.

claim: Members of the NF-kB signaling pathways have been proposed as therapeutic targets for inflammatory diseases and cancers.
source: Members of the NF-kB signaling pathways have been proposed as therapeutic targets for inflammatory diseases and cancers, with various types of inhibitors being developed.
evidence: The statement is based on general knowledge of NF-kB pathway.

claim: Copy number amplifications of 11q22 and 3q25 (where YAP1 and WWTR1 are located, respectively) are common events reported in OSCC, often in mutual exclusive manner.
source: Copy number amplifications of 11q22 and 3q25 (where YAP1 and WWTR1 are located, respectively) are common events reported in OSCC, often in mutual exclusive manner (Campbell et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: YAP1 had a more prominent role in transcriptional regulation than WWTR1 in OSCC.
source: Analysis of genome-wide transcriptional changes upon knockdown of YAP1 or WWTR1 in OSCC showed that YAP1 had a more prominent role in transcriptional regulation (Hiemer et al., 2015).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Hiemer et al., 2015.

claim: YAP1 acted as a strong driver in OSCC tumor initiation and progression in a tongue orthotopic mouse model with the deletion of MOB1A/B.
source: Using a tongue orthotopic mouse model with the deletion of MOB1A/B, Omori et al., 2020 provided strong evidence that YAP1 acted as a strong driver in OSCC tumor initiation and progression, whereby WWTR1 did not seems to play an equivalent role (Omori et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Omori et al., 2020.

claim: Overexpression of PIK3CA was shown to be correlated with YAP1 activation and associated with poor clinical outcome.
source: Overexpression of PIK3CA was shown to be correlated with YAP1 activation and associated with poor clinical outcome (García-Escudero et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to García-Escudero et al., 2018.

claim: The activation of the PI3K through mitogenic signaling inhibits the Hippo pathway leading to YAP1 activation and cell growth.
source: Further, the activation of the PI3K through mitogenic signaling inhibits the Hippo pathway leading to YAP1 activation and cell growth (Fan et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2013.

claim: WWTR1 was shown to act upstream of SOX2, facilitating stemnesses in HNSCC.
source: On the other hand, WWTR1 was shown to act upstream of SOX2, facilitating stemnesses in HNSCC (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: WWTR1 knockdown led to reduction of SOX2 mRNA and protein expression, but this was not seen when YAP1 was knockdown in the HNSCC cells (Cal27 and Fadu).
source: Intriguingly, while WWTR1 knockdown led to reduction of SOX2 mRNA and protein expression, this was not seen when YAP1 was knockdown in the HNSCC cells (Cal27 and Fadu) (Li et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2017.

claim: An inverse relationship between the expression levels of YAP1 and ΔNp63 were reported in lung SCC tumor samples.
source: In support of that, an inverse relationship between the expression levels of YAP1 and ΔNp63 were reported in lung SCC tumor samples (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2017.

claim: The inverse relationship between YAP1 and ΔNp63 expression was not seen in HNSCC tumor samples and cell lines.
source: However, this was not seen in HNSCC tumor samples and cell lines (Ge et al., 2011), suggesting a cancer/context-specific regulatory mechanism might be in place.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Ge et al., 2011.

claim: p63, together with the co-expressing chromotin remodeling factor, ACTL6A, can drive YAP1 activation, suppressing differentiation and promoting cell proliferation in HNSCC.
source: Consistent with the oncogenic roles of YAP1 reported in OSCC (Hiemer et al., 2015; Omori et al., 2020), another study showed that p63, together with the co-expressing chromotin remodeling factor, ACTL6A, can drive YAP1 activation, suppressing differentiation and promoting cell proliferation in HNSCC (Saladi et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Hiemer et al., 2015; Omori et al., 2020; Saladi et al., 2017.

claim: Current inhibitors of YAP1 such as verteporfin and CA3 that blocks its interactions with the TEAD transcription factors also targets WWTR1.
source: Current inhibitors of YAP1 such as verteporfin and CA3 that blocks its interactions with the TEAD transcription factors also targets WWTR1 (Song et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015); therefore, this data underscores the need to develop more specific inhibitors to prevent the targeting of many different downstream pathways.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Song et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: YAP1 and WWTR1 could mediate mutant PIK3CA-induced tumorigenesis.
source: As recent studies have provided evidence that YAP1 and WWTR1 could mediate mutant PIK3CA-induced tumorigenesis (Zhao et al., 2018) andother studies also suggested crosstalk between these Hippo pathway effectors with the PI3K-Akt pathway (García-Escudero et al., 2018), confirmatory and mechanistic studies will be needed to delineate why YAP1 and WWTR1 function can be compensated in these PIK3CA-mutated cell lines, while distinct dependencies on either paralog are observed in PIK3CA wild-type lines.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2018; García-Escudero et al., 2018.

claim: The functional loss of mutated FAT1 has been reported to be associated with YAP1 activation in head and neck cancer.
source: The functional loss of mutated FAT1 has also been reported to be associated with YAP1 activation in head and neck cancer (Martin et al., 2018), however, no enrichment of FAT1 mutation was seen among the YAP1-dependent nor WWTR1-dependent models in this study.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 2018.

claim: The inactivation of the Hippo pathway through the loss of LATS1/2 was reported to cause the induction of anti-tumor immune response and inhibition of HNSCC tumor growth, via the hyperactivation of YAP1/WWTR1.
source: The inactivation of the Hippo pathway through the loss of LATS1/2 was reported to cause the induction of anti-tumor immune response and inhibition of HNSCC tumor growth, via the hyperactivation of YAP1/WWTR1 (Barth et al., 2013; Moroishi et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Barth et al., 2013; Moroishi et al., 2016.

claim: Constitutively active WWTR1 induces PD-L1 expression to a greater extent than YAP1.
source: Specifically, WWTR1 but not YAP1 was shown to be essential for TH17 cell differentiation (Geng et al., 2017), and constitutively active WWTR1 (TAZ-S89A) was shown to induce PD-L1 expression to a much greater extent than YAP1 (YAP1-S127A) (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Geng et al., 2017; Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018.

claim: WWTR1 but not YAP1 was shown to be essential for TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Specifically, WWTR1 but not YAP1 was shown to be essential for TH17 cell differentiation (Geng et al., 2017), and constitutively active WWTR1 (TAZ-S89A) was shown to induce PD-L1 expression to a much greater extent than YAP1 (YAP1-S127A) (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2017.

claim: Tumors with YAP1 amplifications have low T-cell infiltration.
source: This finding is consistent with the recent discovery that constitutively active WWTR1 induces PD-L1 expression, to a greater extent than YAP1 (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018), and that tumors with YAP1 amplifications have low T-cell infiltration (Saloura et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Janse van Rensburg et al., 2018; Saloura et al., 2019.

claim: The number of significantly depleted genes ranged from 525 genes in ORL-156 to 1399 genes in ORL-215 at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%.
source: At a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%, the number of significantly depleted genes ranged from 525 genes in ORL-156 to 1399 genes in ORL-215 (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: More than 80% of all the MAGeCK hits were found to be core fitness genes.
source: In general, more than 80% of all the MAGeCK hits were found to be core fitness genes and were filtered out (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: About 60% (552 genes) of the 918 non-core fitness genes were essential in at least two cell lines.
source: About 40% (366 genes) were uniquely essential in a single cell line, while the remaining 60% (552 genes) were essential in at least two cell lines, hence are recurrent context-specific essentialities (Figure 1C).
evidence: The statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only two of nine cell lines with PIK3CA copy number amplification are dependent on PIK3CA itself.
source: Only two of nine cell lines with PIK3CA copy number amplification are dependent on PIK3CA itself.
evidence: The statement is based on analysis of copy number and dependency data.

claim: Copy number amplification of WWTR1 may constitute to a functional oncogenic role of WWTR1 in OSCC, instead of being a passenger gene that is co-amplified with the canonical HNSCC oncogene, PIK3CA.
source: This suggests that copy number amplification of WWTR1 may constitute to a functional oncogenic role of WWTR1 in OSCC, instead of being a passenger gene that is co-amplified with the canonical HNSCC oncogene, PIK3CA.
evidence: The statement is based on analysis of copy number and dependency data.

claim: YAP1-dependent lines have higher YAP1 expression.
source: Generally, cell lines that are dependent on YAP1 have higher YAP1 expression, and similarly, WWTR1-dependent lines have higher expression of WWTR1 compared to YAP1.
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression analysis of cell lines.

claim: WWTR1-dependent lines have higher expression of WWTR1 compared to YAP1.
source: Generally, cell lines that are dependent on YAP1 have higher YAP1 expression, and similarly, WWTR1-dependent lines have higher expression of WWTR1 compared to YAP1.
evidence: The statement is based on gene expression analysis of cell lines.

claim: WWTR1 gene expression showed significant negative correlation with its dependency in 273 cancer cell lines (Pearson R = −0.570, p-value=3e-25).
source: WWTR1 gene expression showed significant negative correlation with its dependency in these 273 cancer cell lines (Pearson R = −0.570, p-value=3e-25) and showed non-significant negative correlation among our 21 OSCC lines screened (Pearson R = −0.354, p-value=0.116) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: WWTR1 gene expression showed non-significant negative correlation with its dependency among 21 OSCC lines screened (Pearson R = −0.354, p-value=0.116).
source: WWTR1 gene expression showed significant negative correlation with its dependency in these 273 cancer cell lines (Pearson R = −0.570, p-value=3e-25) and showed non-significant negative correlation among our 21 OSCC lines screened (Pearson R = −0.354, p-value=0.116) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: Non-small cell lung carcinoma showed the highest percentage of WWTR1-dependency (30%) among cancers with negative correlation between WWTR1 expression and dependency.
source: Among these cancers, non-small cell lung carcinoma showed the highest percentage of WWTR1-dependency (30%), with the strongest correlation (Pearson's R = −0.934, p-value=0.0021).
evidence: The statement is based on analysis of Project Score data.

claim: SAS harbors a fusion protein of YAP1 and MAML2.
source: Besides, another YAP1-dependent line, SAS has recently been reported to harbor a fusion protein of YAP1 and MAML2 (Picco et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Picco et al., 2019.

claim: CTGF and CYR61 are two canonical transcriptional targets of YAP1 and WWTR1 in OSCC.
source: In OSCC, CTGF, and CYR61 are two canonical transcriptional targets of YAP1 and WWTR1 (Hiemer et al., 2015).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Hiemer et al., 2015.

claim: More substantial reduction of CTGF and CYR61 gene expression were seen only when the respective upstream fitness genes were knocked-out.
source: Consistent with their known pro-survival properties, more substantial reduction of CTGF and CYR61 gene expression were seen only when the respective upstream fitness genes were knocked-out, as measured by qPCR (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: The statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4F.

claim: YAP1 depletion in ORL-48 resulted in increased apoptosis.
source: Consistently, YAP1 depletion in ORL-48 resulted in significant reduction in viable cells, to a level comparable to the depletion of PLK1 (Figure 4A), and this was reflected in the increase in apoptotic cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The statement is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WWTR1 depletion in ORL-214 resulted in significant increase in apoptotic cells.
source: Further, WWTR1 depletion in ORL-214 showed significantly lower percentage of viable cells when compared with the control, as well as significant increase in apoptotic cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The statement is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Strong suppression of CTGF and CYR61 gene expression in BICR10 and HSC-2 is only seen when YAP1 and WWTR1 are simultaneously knocked-out.
source: This was substantiated by quantitative-PCR (qPCR) of downstream targets CTGF and CYR61 where substantial down-regulation in double knockout cells were observed compared to when each gene is knocked-out individually (Figure 5C).
evidence: The statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 18-gene T-cell inflamed GEP is a clinically validated biomarker of response towards pembrolizumab in HNSCC clinical trial.
source: Single-sample GSEA (ssGSEA) was performed using the GenePatterns web-tool (https://www.genepattern.org/) (Reich et al., 2006) with the 18-genes T-cell inflamed Gene Expression Profile (GEP) gene set, which was found to be predictive biomarkers for response to pembrolizumab in HNSCC clinical trial (Ayers et al., 2017; Cristescu et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Reich et al., 2006; Ayers et al., 2017; Cristescu et al., 2018.
